evidence.estrutura: Her Abeokuta organizing emphasized local women’s collective power against colonial and traditional authority, supporting decentralized/community participation.
evidence.representacao: Campaigns for women’s political rights and participation strongly support democratic inclusion.
evidence.poder: Anti-colonial organizing and resistance to abusive taxation and authority place her against unaccountable coercion.
evidence.imigracao: Her politics centered anti-colonial equality rather than immigration law; Pan-African and anti-colonial commitments support pluralist solidarity.
evidence.diplomacia: She participated in international and Pan-African networks, favoring political solidarity over militarist nationalism.
evidence.intervencao: Anti-colonial activism strongly supports self-determination and opposition to foreign domination.
evidence.economia: Campaigns against unfair taxation and for women’s economic conditions support redistribution and social-economic reform rather than laissez-faire.
evidence.controle: Collective organization and social reform support moderate public/community coordination, not centralized command planning.
evidence.comercio: Colonial economic critique suggests skepticism toward extractive external commerce, but no detailed tariff doctrine.
evidence.religiao: Her political organizing was civic and anti-colonial rather than clerical; moderately secular public orientation.
evidence.moral: Women’s rights and resistance to gender discrimination strongly support progressive equality.
evidence.tecnologia: Technology was not a defining issue; moderate modernist.
